extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys, Patent Office officials, and judges handling patent appeals
extracted.subtask_description: Judicial opinions on appeals from the U.S. Commissioner of Patents resolving priority disputes and related procedural/evidentiary questions; sets standards for admissibility of evidence, reduction to practice, diligence/abandonment, and the scope of judicial review on such appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of judicial review on appeal (Act of March 3, 1839, §11)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner of Patents is to 'lay before the judge all the original papers and evidence in the case, together with the grounds of his decision fully set forth in writing touching all the points involved by the reasons of appeal, to which the revision shall be confined.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The judge's revision on appeal is confined to the original papers, evidence, and the points involved by the reasons of appeal and the grounds of the Commissioner's decision. The judge should consider only those matters presented in that record when reviewing the Commissioner's decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of depositions taken without notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Depositions taken without notice to an applicant (i.e., taken in proceedings before other applicants without notice to a later applicant) 'cannot be used against him, unless he has waived his right to notice, and agreed to admit them to be read in evidence before the Commissioner of Patents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If depositions were taken without giving the affected applicant notice, they are inadmissible against that applicant unless there is an explicit waiver. Mere inspection of depositions by counsel and an offer to produce them for inspection is not necessarily a waiver; refusal to cross-examine when witnesses are later produced is not equivalent to a waiver of the right to notice. On appeal, the judge will reject such depositions as evidence against the unnotified applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of Patent Office officer at judicial hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer of the Patent Office may attend hearings before the judge on appeals 'for the purpose of explaining the decision of the Commissioner,' and is not to be considered counsel or an advocate for either party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Office officers may appear before the judge to explain the Commissioner's decision and assist in investigating the truth, but they should not act as advocates for either litigant. The judge may avail himself of the officer's assistance in understanding the administrative decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining priority: evidence must show conception of the same invention
rubrics_metrics.description: In a priority contest the question is 'which, or whether either, of these applicants is entitled to receive the patent prayed for;' the inquiry is whether the earlier description/conception is 'substantially the same' as that for which a patent is now claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To award priority, the court examines the evidence produced before the Commissioner to determine whether the earlier conception/description corresponds substantially to the claimed invention. The judge compares the specification/claims with the prior descriptions/drawings to see if they describe the same essential features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to practice (descriptive/constructive standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor has reduced his invention to practice 'when he has so described it upon paper, with such drawings or model as to enable any person, skilled in the art, to make and use the same.' He must show that it is practicable and the manner in which it may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction to practice does not require physical construction or use; a sufficiently detailed written description and drawings or a model that enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention constitute reduction to practice. The description must render the principle practicable and clearly point out how it may be made useful so a competent mechanic can avail himself of it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to practice vs. actual use before patent
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Reducing to practice differs from bringing into use. There is no law requiring the applicant to reduce his invention to actual use before he can obtain a patent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing and supporting materials showing practicability suffice for patentability even if the invention was never actually used prior to application. Conversely, earlier public or commercial use of the invention before application may be a separate ground for refusing a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor's description may suffice even if machine not built
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inventor 'described the machine ... so that [a witness] perfectly understood it' and produced drawings enabling construction and costing, 'Cornell made the invention as clearly understood as if the machine had been built and in operation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed sketches and explanations that allow a skilled mechanic to construct the device can establish an inventor's priority even where the inventor never actually built the machine; the mechanical labor of construction is distinct from the inventive conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning and limits of dictum 'first to reduce to practice is first inventor'
rubrics_metrics.description: The opinion rejects the broad dictum that 'he who first reduces an invention to practice is the first inventor' as not the law in broad terms; reduction to practice must be taken in the sense that it renders a principle practicable and clearly points out how to make it useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court clarifies that the phrase 'reduce to practice' should be read to mean a constructive reduction (adequate description enabling practice) rather than requiring actual prior construction or use; cases that state the dictum without this qualification may be misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable diligence clause (§15) limited application
rubrics_metrics.description: The clause about loss of benefit from delay (equity of the fifteenth section of the patent law of 1836) is 'only applicable to the case of a patent surreptitiously or unjustly obtained while the first inventor was using reasonable diligence in adapting and perfecting his invention; not to the case of conflicting applicants before any patent is granted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The equitable defense that a later applicant unjustly obtained a patent while the first inventor was diligently perfecting the invention applies only after a patent has been issued and in suits to vacate it. It does not bar an earlier inventor from obtaining a patent absent evidence of abandonment or surreptitious procurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment by lapse of time is a factual question for jury
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no law requiring disclosure within any time limit; 'the lapse of time [must be] sufficient to show an abandonment of the invention, which is a question for the jury and not for the Commissioner.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay alone does not automatically constitute abandonment; whether a delay amounts to abandonment is a factual determination appropriate for a jury in later litigation (e.g., infringement/defense), not for the Commissioner on initial patent grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of application does not decide priority of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The opinion states that 'the priority of application for a patent does not decide the priority of invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Who filed first is not decisive of who invented first; priority of invention is determined by the substantive evidence of conception and reduction to practice (in the constructive sense), not merely the filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative standard for evidence before Commissioner vs. courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings before the Commissioner 'are initiatory. The question is, "whether the patent shall be granted," not "whether it shall be vacated;" and a patent may be granted or refused upon less evidence than would be required to sustain or amend it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commissioner may decide patentability on a lower quantum or quality of evidence than a court would require to sustain a patent in litigation. Judicial review is limited to the record, and the standards in the administrative grant context differ from those applied in later legal challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between testimony about working machine and time of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Witnesses may 'speak of the time when the invention was first applied to a machine in operation, not to the time of the invention itself, which necessarily precedes it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing priority, differentiate testimony about when an improvement was first put into use (which may postdate conception) from testimony about when the inventor conceived or described the invention; the latter is the relevant time for priority of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative/credibility weighing of conflicting testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: When a witness gives a date contradicted by other circumstances, the court may find the witness erred and give less credence: 'the whole of the testimony shows that this machine was not put in operation until the month of July, 1845, subsequent to the time at which the witness testifies the said improvement was described to him ... [the Commissioner] erred in giving credence to the statement by a witness of a date, which all the circumstances ... clearly shows was the result of error.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate witness credibility against the totality of circumstantial evidence; positive testimony that aligns with circumstances may outweigh inconsistent statements. The court may discount testimony where surrounding facts clearly show an error in claimed dates or recollection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural sufficiency in priority appeals (need not detail every alteration)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a mere priority contest 'it is not necessary to describe the particular alterations of the old machine which constitute the improvement' when the only question is priority of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the appeal only concerns who first invented an improvement, it may be unnecessary to enter into granular mechanical detail of every alteration; the focus is on whether the earlier conception disclosed the essential distinguishing features of the claimed improvement.
